newsitem.title: CHINA: China vows to crack down on security leaks.
newsitem.headline: China vows to crack down on security leaks.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin has vowed to crack down on people who leak state secrets, saying security issues are essential to economic growth, the official People's Daily said on Saturday.
"In this new historical era, how we handle security work directly affects the development of reform and opening up and modernisation," the Communist Party mouthpiece quoted Jiang as saying.
China would take initial steps in implementing regulations governing secrets and setting up a system aimed at enforcing those rules by the year 2000, the newspaper said.
"As for cases of leaking state secrets, we must be strict in investigating and handling them, resolutely striking according to the law," it quoted Jiang as saying.
"We must absolutely not be lenient or abet the evil by tolerating it," Jiang said.
"We must pay 100 percent attention to protecting party secrets. Ninety-five percent is not enough, 99 percent is not enough. Anything other than 100 percent is unacceptable," he said.
Jiang did not elaborate on what specific measures would be taken to counter security lapses.
China's broad definition of state secrets includes some economic and financial information -- much of which would be considered public information in the West.

Beijing earlier this year detained a Chinese national employed by Royal Dutch/Shell Group and her counterpart from a mainland oil company on what was believed to be suspicion of obtaining state secrets linked to an oil refinery project.
In September, authorities detained an employee of SBC Warburg, apparently for having helped prepare materials for company clients on the trend of China's currency, the yuan.

A China-born journalist working for a Hong Kong newspaper was sentenced to 12 years in prison in 1994 for allegedly stealing state secrets, believed to have been reports on interest rate trends and gold sales.
Many foreign businessmen have said they are troubled by the detentions and are concerned about what duties their local employees can undertake without breaking Chinese law.
